solutions.check: 29 entries; each light the paper's grid did not give solved here from its clue's wordplay (an anagram or hidden word, the one listed word fitting every crossing) and its definition (WordNet), as the answer another puzzle gave the same clue, or as the one past answer its crossings left that the printed letters allow, agrees with the 28 answers the paper printed

clue.text: Blouse damaged by dagger

indicators.note: something damaged is knocked out of shape, so the letters of the blouse are rearranged

explanation.surface: A blouse has been slashed by someone wielding a dagger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dagger' reads as a weapon, but printers also use the name for the dagger mark, one of the reference signs.
explanation.definitionFit: The obelus is a printer's reference mark, the obelisk or dagger sign used for footnotes.

clue.text: Prohibit one including Italian singer

indicators.note: including means taking in, so the joined words enclose the abbreviation for Italian

parts.note: prohibit means bar
taken as written

explanation.surface: Ban an Italian from singing, including that one.
explanation.definitionFit: A baritone is a male vocalist with a voice between tenor and bass.

clue.text: This popular if non-U part of Italy

explanation.surface: A region of Italy is said to be well liked if not upper-class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'popular' without its U gives POPLAR, and the Lombardy poplar is the familiar tall columnar tree; 'non-U' also teases as British slang for not upper-class.
explanation.definitionFit: The northern Italian region around Milan gives its name to the tall columnar poplar tree.

clue.text: Periodical shows unusual tact in prose composition

indicators.note: in places the shuffled tact inside the shuffled prose
composition means putting together, so the letters of prose are arranged afresh
unusual signals that the letters of tact appear in an odd order

explanation.surface: A magazine displays unusual diplomacy in its written essays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shows' is only a link. 'unusual' scrambles one word and 'composition' the other, and 'in' sets the first inside the second.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spectator is a long-running British weekly magazine, a type of journal.

clue.text: More than enough for a graduate -wicked!

parts.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts, is the usual abbreviation for a graduate
wicked means sinful

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims that a university graduate has been given far too much of something.
explanation.definitionFit: A basinful is an informal British idiom for a surfeit, as in having had a basinful of complaints.

clue.text: But inadequate top cover for one in six hundred

definitions.text: But inadequate top cover for one in six hundred

parts.words: But inadequate top cover for one in six hundred
parts.note: the six hundred are the Light Brigade of Tennyson's poem, who charged at a Crimean battle; their woollen headgear gave little protection

explanation.surface: A hat offered too little protection to one soldier among hundreds.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's 'Charge of the Light Brigade' calls the cavalry 'the six hundred'; the knitted head covering is named after that 1854 Crimean battle.
explanation.definitionFit: This knitted woollen hood covering head and neck takes its name from the Crimean War battle of the Light Brigade.

clue.text: Set apart one the sun-god consumed

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
Sol was the Roman god of the sun
consumed means ate

explanation.surface: One person was cut off after being devoured by the solar deity.
explanation.definitionFit: To isolate is to separate something or someone from others.

clue.text: Enthusiast's on the ball with this act

indicators.note: on means placed on top, so in this down entry the enthusiast sits above the ball

parts.note: an enthusiast is a fan
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: A keen supporter is alert and alongside this performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the ball' reads as alert, but 'ball' is a dance and 'on' stacks the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A fan dance is a burlesque stage routine performed behind large feather fans.

clue.text: Flower birds turn up on river

parts.note: larks are songbirds

indicators.note: turn means the little word up is turned around

parts.note: R is the map abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Birds turn upwards over a stream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' reverses UP to PU.
explanation.definitionFit: Larkspur is a garden plant with spurred blue flowers, a kind of delphinium.

clue.text: London's road protector

explanation.surface: A London street is being described as a guardian.
explanation.walkthrough: Cromwell Road is a major road in west London; Oliver Cromwell ruled England as Lord Protector in the 1650s.
explanation.definitionFit: One surname names both a west London thoroughfare and the seventeenth-century Lord Protector who governed after the Civil War.

clue.text: Snug his job — as an army recruit?

explanation.surface: Someone has a cosy post, perhaps as a new soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: A carpenter's craftsman makes joints that fit snugly; and a recruit is one who joins the army, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A woodworker who fits joints together tightly, and jokingly anyone who signs up or enlists.

clue.text: Mrs Partington's main opponent

parts.note: Mrs Partington, in a famous 1831 jibe by Sydney Smith, tried to mop back a storm tide from her Devon doorstep; 'main' hints at the sea itself

explanation.surface: A lady's chief rival is being named.
explanation.walkthrough: Sydney Smith compared the Lords resisting reform to Mrs Partington of Sidmouth sweeping back the ocean with a mop; 'main' is an old word for the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The ocean whose storm surge the legendary Mrs Partington tried to sweep away is the one off the English west coast.

clue.text: State is without a port

indicators.note: without here has its old sense of outside, so the state and the word is surround the a

parts.note: CAL is an abbreviation for the US state of California
taken as written

explanation.surface: A country lacks any harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking', but here it has its old meaning, 'outside'.
explanation.definitionFit: Calais is the French Channel ferry harbour facing Dover.

clue.text: Subject to "income' tax?

parts.note: the quotes make 'income' mean goods coming in, so the levy is a customs charge on imports

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether something is liable to income tax.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'income' as things coming in to the country: imported goods are liable to customs charges.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods liable to customs or excise charges are taxable on import.

clue.text: Curious getting £500 change? Absurd!

indicators.note: change means alter, so the letters of curious and the money are reshuffled together

parts.note: £ is L, from the Latin libra, and 500 is D in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Someone inquisitive gets five hundred pounds in change and finds it ridiculous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' shuffles CURIOUS with L (the pound sign) and D (500).
explanation.definitionFit: Ludicrous means ridiculous or laughably foolish.

clue.text: Raising of troops that could reduce our capital

explanation.surface: Mustering soldiers might drain the nation's funds.
explanation.walkthrough: A levy is both a conscription of soldiers and a tax, such as a capital charge on wealth.
explanation.definitionFit: One word means both the conscription of soldiers and a compulsory charge on wealth.

clue.text: Body-binder of dressing material used outside sporting contest

indicators.note: used outside means the dressing material goes around the contest

parts.note: lint is a fabric used to dress wounds
a game is a sporting contest

explanation.surface: A piece of wound dressing is worn over clothes at a sports match.
explanation.definitionFit: A ligament is a band of tough tissue that ties bones together in the body.

clue.text: Direction of take-off in this plane

definitions.text: Direction of take-off in this plane

parts.words: Direction of take-off in this plane
parts.note: a jump jet rises straight up; 'this plane' also means the up-and-down line of a grid entry going downwards

explanation.surface: Someone asks which way this aircraft lifts off.
explanation.walkthrough: Plane means both aircraft and flat geometric surface; the answer itself is a down entry, running upright.
explanation.definitionFit: Straight upward and perpendicular to the horizon describes both a jump jet's lift-off and an upright geometric plane.

clue.text: Resort in South Devon to drink

explanation.surface: A seaside spot in the south of England is somewhere to have a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Beer is a small fishing village and resort on the south Devon coast, Devon being a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: A Devon coastal village shares its name with the brewed alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: Better perhaps putting in duck's eggs as part of the salad

indicators.note: perhaps hints at a possible variant, so the letters of better and the eggs are rearranged

parts.note: a duck in cricket is a score of zero, whose shape is an egg, so two of them give two O letters

explanation.surface: A gambler may add duck eggs as part of a salad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges BETTER plus OO; a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, like an egg-shaped O.
explanation.definitionFit: Beetroot is a dark red root vegetable often served sliced in salads.

clue.text: This book, Smith Minor, is not about physical training

definitions.text: This book, Smith Minor, is not about physical training

parts.words: This book, Smith Minor, is not about physical training
parts.note: Smith Minor is the younger Smith boy at a British school, and the pupil's book here is for written work, not gym

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster tells a younger pupil that his book has nothing to do with PE.
explanation.walkthrough: British schools call the younger of two brothers 'Minor'; the schoolroom writing book shares its name with physical activity.
explanation.definitionFit: A school exercise book holds written practice work, while the same word also means a physical workout.

clue.text: Nothing terribly grand that is material

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

indicators.note: terribly suggests something badly mangled, so the word grand is rearranged

parts.note: i.e., id est, means that is

explanation.surface: Something is called terribly grand, though it is merely physical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing' gives a letter, not an absence, and 'terribly' tells you to rearrange the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Organdie is a fine, stiff, sheer cotton fabric.

clue.text: A nice company formation describes the South Sea Bubble

indicators.note: formation means a new arrangement, so a nice and the company letters are reformed

explanation.surface: A pleasant firm is founded, recalling the eighteenth-century South Sea Bubble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'formation' rearranges A NICE with CO; the South Sea Bubble was a 1720 British financial crash, here read as a bubble on the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Oceanic means belonging to the sea, as a bubble on the South Seas would be.

clue.text: National cause of uprising

parts.note: not a revolution: the national song makes everyone rise to their feet

explanation.surface: Something sparks a nationwide revolt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uprising' looks political, but it is the crowd standing up when the national song plays.
explanation.definitionFit: A country's official song is played while people stand respectfully.

clue.text: Stretched the centre to full length and so on

definitions.text: Stretched the centre to full length

explanation.surface: Something was extended right out from its middle, and so forth.
explanation.walkthrough: The centre of 'Stretched' holds ETC; stretched to full length that abbreviation becomes the full Latin phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase meaning 'and the rest' is used to show a list continues.

clue.text: Oriental one embraced the church in ancient time

parts.note: E, east, stands for oriental

indicators.note: embraced means held within, so the word one wraps around the letters for the church

parts.note: taken as written
CE, the Church of England, stands for the church

explanation.surface: An Eastern person adopted the Christian church long ago.
explanation.definitionFit: The Eocene is a geological epoch of about 56 to 34 million years ago.

clue.text: Flower of remembrance? This is so, to my embarrassment

indicators.note: embarrassment suggests confusion and disorder, so the letters of is so to my are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone admits with embarrassment that something to do with a remembrance flower is true.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embarrassment' rearranges IS SO TO MY.
explanation.definitionFit: Myosotis is the botanical genus of the forget-me-not, a flower whose name asks to be remembered.

clue.text: Eg a TV play, or its players

explanation.surface: A small-screen drama is mentioned, or perhaps its actors.
explanation.walkthrough: A broadcast on television; read as TELE CAST it is the actors of the telly.
explanation.definitionFit: A television broadcast; split in two it is the company of actors performing on the telly.

clue.text: Fabric observed wrapped round a cat's tail

indicators.note: wrapped round means the word observed encloses the next two pieces

parts.note: observed means seen

indicators.note: a word's tail is its final letter

explanation.surface: Some cloth was seen wound around the end of a cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Sateen is a glossy cotton cloth woven to imitate satin.
